raw_plan.interpretation: I interpret this as one acquisition email for agency or freelance developers evaluating a repeatable analytics option for client sites. The reader relationship is unknown, so the email will address the audience-level decision without assuming a current analytics stack, client problem or prior failure.

intent.desired_action: Start a free self-serve evaluation and review the installation approach for one representative website.

raw_plan.reader: An agency or freelance developer assessing whether Simple Analytics could be a privacy-friendly analytics option for suitable client websites.
raw_plan.reader_segment: Agency or freelance developer choosing the analytics stack for client sites
raw_plan.reader_scope: Developers evaluating analytics for client sites where avoiding cookies, trackers, visitor-consent collection and personal-data processing matters. Recipient fit and permission to deploy on any client site remain unverified.
raw_plan.promise: Simple Analytics gives developers a documented way to provide useful website analytics without cookies, trackers or personal-data processing, with installation guidance adapted to each website's technology.
raw_plan.orientation: Simple Analytics is a cookie-free website analytics option for agencies and freelance developers evaluating a repeatable default across client sites, with per-site installation and documented privacy conditions.
raw_plan.arc: Move from skepticism about broad privacy-friendly claims to the specific product design behind Simple Analytics, then invite a scoped self-serve evaluation for one representative website.
raw_plan.sequence_rationale: With only one email, the strongest argument is the defining operational benefit supported by the dossier: analytics that requires no cookies, trackers or visitor consent and does not process personal data. The brief answers the audience's documented skepticism with product behavior rather than a generic compliance label. Technology-dependent installation is attached as a condition of adopting that benefit, not treated as a separate reason to buy. The CTA is a scoped evaluation rather than a portfolio-wide commitment because client-site permissions, plan limits and aggregate agency economics are not established. The GA4 proof of concept is preserved as a complete alternative for the narrower situation where a client already uses GA4. The single thing that would most change this campaign is a readable copy of the unavailable Simple Analytics source page.

emails.selection_reason: The audience research shows developers disputing whether privacy-friendly analytics actually avoids consent requirements. The product's documented absence of cookies, trackers and personal-data processing directly addresses that decision and is more broadly relevant than assuming the reader currently uses GA4.

value_case.reader_benefit: For a suitable client website, the developer can provide website analytics without adding cookies or trackers or processing visitors' personal data, reducing the analytics-related consent and DPA questions created by those practices.
value_case.mechanism: Simple Analytics states that it uses no cookies or trackers, requires no visitor consent and does not process personal data. During onboarding, it scans the website's technology and provides a corresponding installation option.
decision_conditions: The no-DPA statement rests on Simple Analytics' documented absence of personal-data processing and its stated GDPR basis; it is not a universal legal opinion for every client or jurisdiction.
Installation is per website and depends on the technology detected.
Client permission and suitability must be established before deployment.

claim_conditions: Describe the privacy benefit as Simple Analytics' documented product behavior, not a universal legal guarantee.
Keep the evaluation scoped to a representative website rather than an entire client portfolio.
Installation instructions vary with the website's detected technology.

emails.job: Get the reader to consider Simple Analytics for a suitable client build and begin a scoped self-serve evaluation.
emails.single_idea: Simple Analytics can give a suitable client website useful analytics without cookies, trackers or personal-data processing, and its onboarding provides installation guidance based on that site's technology.
emails.felt_need: A privacy-friendly label is not enough; the developer needs to know whether the analytics implementation actually uses cookies, trackers or personal data that could reintroduce consent and DPA questions.
emails.status_quo: Developers compare named analytics tools and debate whether their privacy claims genuinely remove the need for visitor consent.
emails.why_it_fails: A broad privacy-friendly claim does not reveal whether the product still uses identifiers, cookies or personal data—the mechanisms at the center of the consent debate.
emails.mechanism: Simple Analytics documents no cookies, no trackers and no personal-data processing. When evaluating a site, its onboarding scans the technology and supplies an appropriate installation option; the code still has to be added through the relevant site or platform route.

alternative_arguments.selection_reason: This is a strong alternative for the narrower case where a client already uses GA4: an assisted comparison on the client's own site can inform a measurement decision without requiring an immediate switch.

value_case.reader_benefit: If a suitable client already uses GA4, the developer can compare weekly pageview trends on that client's own site and review methodological causes behind differences before deciding whether Simple Analytics belongs in the measurement setup.
value_case.mechanism: The assisted proof of concept begins by defining a measurement question, then runs Simple Analytics alongside GA4 for 30 days and reviews differences against factors including duplicate tags, SPA routing, bot filtering, consent configuration and reporting identity.
decision_conditions: This route applies only when an assisted comparison alongside GA4 is relevant.
The proof of concept requires booking a demo and keeping GA4 and the existing consent setup in place during the comparison.
The review does not promise an isolated consent-rejection figure.

claim_conditions: Present this as a conditional option for sites already using GA4.
Keep the 30-day duration attached to the assisted proof of concept.
Do not imply that the comparison automatically identifies one definitive cause for a pageview difference.
alternative_arguments.single_idea: For a client already using GA4, Simple Analytics offers an assisted 30-day side-by-side comparison built around a defined measurement question rather than asking for an immediate switch.
alternative_arguments.felt_need: If two analytics systems report different totals, the useful question is what methodological factors explain the difference—not whether one headline number is larger.
alternative_arguments.status_quo: A team may compare reported GA4 and Simple Analytics totals for the same site and period.
alternative_arguments.why_it_fails: The raw gap alone cannot distinguish consent configuration from tag coverage, routing, bot filtering, duplicate events or reporting identity.
alternative_arguments.mechanism: After a scoping discussion, both systems run alongside each other for 30 days. Weekly trends are reviewed against the documented methodological causes.
alternative_arguments.belief_shift: Before: a meaningful evaluation requires accepting or rejecting Simple Analytics on headline claims. After: an assisted comparison can test a defined measurement question on the client's own site while preserving the existing setup.
must_not_say: Do not claim the proof of concept isolates a consent-rejection rate.
Do not promise that Simple Analytics will report more pageviews or reveal a specific cause.
Do not describe the assisted proof of concept as self-serve.
Do not assume the recipient or every client currently uses GA4.
alternative_arguments.objection: We cannot judge another analytics tool from a generic demo or an unexplained difference in totals.
alternative_arguments.call_to_action: Book a demo to define the measurement question for a free 30-day proof of concept alongside GA4.
alternative_arguments.next_step_decision: Decide whether a side-by-side evaluation would answer a concrete measurement question for a client already using GA4.
alternative_arguments.next_step_value: The demo starts with a discussion of the GA4 setup and the question to compare, establishing the scope for an assisted 30-day proof of concept.
alternative_arguments.next_step_limit: Booking the demo does not produce the comparison result, and the completed review does not promise to isolate consent rejection as a single quantified cause.
alternative_arguments.subject_strategy: Frame a low-commitment, side-by-side measurement decision for readers with a relevant GA4 site; avoid promising a switch, uplift or consent-gap figure.
